To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the gene expression analysis of Dark Agouta rats 3 weeks after a single dose of 3,4-Methylenedioxy-methamphetamine (MDM, "Ecstasy") indicates upregulation of cannabinoid CB1 receptor and ephrin receptor gene expression in the hippocampus as well as neurotoxic effects and upregulated synapse-related gene expression in the frontal cortex.
1. Gene expression analysis of the Dark Agouti hippocampus and frontal cortex 3-weeks after MDMA administration reveals a large number of differentially regulated genes.

a single dose of 15 mg/kg MDMA administered to Dark Agouti (DA) rats 3 weeks ago results in the following changes: (1) in the hippocampus the expression of genes related to the regulation of synaptic plasticity is reduced and the expression of cannabinoid receptors is increased; (2) in the frontal cortex genes related to the positive regulation of synapse formation are upregulated, and (3) in the dorsal rapnucleus, no significant change was found.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying the long-term neurobiological and behavioral effects of MDMA.
the molecular mechanisms and the new molecular candidates involved in the long-term impairments caused by a single dose of the neurotoxic drug MDMA.
the molecular changes underlying the cognitive impairments in MDMA users.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present data suggest the involvement of new molecular candidates, which might participate in the long-term cognitive and behavioral impairments after a single dose of the drug.
a single MDMA administration causes long-term alterations in the gene expression in the hippocampus of DA rats, and that the changes in the frontal cortex are less pronounced.

a single dose of 15 mg/kg MDMA causes long-term changes in the gene expression profile of the hippocampus and the frontal cortex of the Dark Agouti rat, which might contribute to the long-term cognitive deficits associated with MDMA use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the long-lasting effects of MDMA on the hippocampus and frontal cortex are mediated by the upregulation and downregulation of genes related to memory, cognition and neurotoxicity, respectively.

a single neurotoxin MDMA dose can induce a long-term depression of new neurites formation in the hippocampi of Dark Agouta rats, which is associated with the upregulation CB1 receptor and ephrin receptor gene expression.

a single neurotoxin dose of MDMA leads to a long-lasting depression in the hippocampus while the frontal cortex is affected with an opposite effect, i.e. a long-lasting increase in gene expression of synapse-related processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the long term neurotoxic effects of a single MDMA dose are more complex than previously thought and involve multiple brain regions and molecular pathways, some of which have not been previously implicated in MDMA neurotoxicity.
a single dose of the drug can lead to a long-lasting molecular changes, which are likely to contribute to the long-term behavioral impairments.
the long-term effects are not restricted to the serotonergic system, but also include other neurotransmitter systems and pathways.
